title: Prescription Assistance
subtitle: Follow the drug from prescription to formulary to final pharmacy cost

blocks.text: A prescription can fit on one screen. Getting it covered may take a formulary, a deductible, special approval and three people saying, “Let me check that.”

Public drug coverage comes mostly from provincial, territorial and federal programs, with private plans on top. National pharmacare deals now cover listed birth control and diabetes products in the four places that have signed on so far. Other medicines still follow local drug plans, drug lists and approval rules.

This lesson follows one prescription from the doctor’s office to the pharmacy counter. You will find out who pays first, read a receipt line by line, see how a deductible year works and learn what to ask before you leave a prescription behind.
National pharmacare is not yet one list for every medicine in every province. It covers listed products where there is a deal, and local public drug plans still matter a lot.

items.text: Coverage for hospital and doctor visits is not the same as coverage for every drug at the pharmacy. Whether you qualify, whether you signed up and the drug list still matter.

blocks.text: Health Canada: National pharmacare coverage
Knowing who pays for your medicine, and how, keeps a surprise bill from putting your treatment at risk.
blocks.detail: The right plan, the drug list and a few price layers decide what you pay at the counter.
blocks.extra: Section 02 helps you find who pays first.

sections.title: Ask Who Pays Before You Ask How Much

blocks.text: Find out who pays before you price the medicine. A claim sent to the wrong door rarely comes back on time.

items.title: PUBLIC PLAN
items.text: Check provincial or territorial plans for seniors, children, people on income support, high drug costs, specific illnesses or coverage based on income.

items.title: FEDERAL PROGRAM
items.text: First Nations and Inuit clients who qualify, veterans, military members, federal workers, refugees and others may have a federal plan with its own rules.

items.title: PRIVATE PLAN
items.text: Coverage through work, a union, retirement, school or your own policy may pay first or work alongside a public plan.

items.title: PATIENT HELP PROGRAMS
items.text: Drug makers or charities may help in some cases. Check the privacy terms, how long it lasts and what happens when the help ends.

blocks.text: When you have two plans, the order matters. Usually your private plan pays first and the public plan picks up part of what is left, but some public plans pay first for certain people. Give the pharmacy every plan card you have and ask which one they billed.

Ontario’s Trillium Drug Program helps households whose drug costs are high compared to their income. Its yearly deductible is about 4% of household income after tax, split into four quarterly amounts. If your income changes by 10% or more, you can ask for a new calculation.

items.title: “If one province covers a drug, every province must cover it.”
items.text: Each province has its own drug list, medical criteria and approval system. Drug names cross borders more easily than payment rules.

blocks.text: Alberta Non-Group Coverage is an optional extra plan for residents under 65 who qualify, and it has a monthly premium. Alberta seniors have a separate plan with no premium.
Ontario: Prescription drug coverage

sections.title: Read the Receipt Like a Drug List, Not a Mood

blocks.text: A pharmacy price is built from parts: the cost of the drug, the pharmacy’s markup and a dispensing fee for filling it. Your plan then pays its share of the parts it covers, and you pay the rest. When the plan’s share is $0, the receipt looks like a mistake even when it is not one.
Here is how a receipt like Dev’s, from the story in Section 05, can add up. The amounts are an example, not a price list. Ask your own pharmacy for its numbers.
$268 + $27 + $15 = $310, and the plan paid $0 because the yearly deductible was not met yet.
blocks.extra: Approval made the drug eligible. The deductible decided who paid first.

items.title: Price at the counter
items.text: Did you ask for this number before the pharmacist filled it?

items.title: Drug cost
items.text: Is a lower-cost version of the same drug on your plan’s list?

items.title: Pharmacy markup
items.text: Does the plan cap the markup, or does another pharmacy charge less?

items.title: Dispensing fee
items.text: How much of the fee does your plan cover, and how often is it charged?

items.title: Paid by the plan
items.text: How much of your family’s deductible is still left this year?

blocks.text: How a deductible year works
Fair PharmaCare in three stages

items.title: Until the deductible
items.text: You pay 100% — of eligible costs, until your family reaches its deductible.

items.title: After the deductible
items.text: 70% / 30% — PharmaCare pays 70% and you pay 30%, until you reach your family maximum.

items.title: After the maximum
items.text: 100% plan — PharmaCare pays all eligible costs for the rest of the calendar year.

blocks.text: Fair PharmaCare sets your deductible and family maximum from your family’s net income two years earlier, and it resets every January. If your income has dropped since then, you can ask for an income review. A lower income on file can lower both numbers.
If you register for Fair PharmaCare but do not agree to the income check, your family is given a $10,000 deductible. Consent is the step that makes the plan fit your income.
If you know your deductible, you can save toward it before January instead of meeting it all at the counter. Try your own numbers below.
Save for next year’s deductible

items.title: Formulary status
items.text: Is this exact drug, strength and form on your plan’s list, and is a lower-cost version covered instead?

items.title: Deductible
items.text: How much do you pay yourself each year before the plan starts sharing the cost?

items.title: Co-payment
items.text: After the deductible, what flat fee or percentage do you pay for each fill?

items.title: Maximum
items.text: Is there a yearly family maximum after which the plan pays more, or a limit on what the plan will pay?

items.title: “Special authorization means the medicine will be free.”
items.text: It can make the drug eligible for the plan to pay. Deductibles, co-payments, price rules and other plans may still apply. Approval opens the door. It does not pay the parking.

blocks.text: B.C.: Fair PharmaCare plan

The federal Pharmacare Act set up a first stage: coverage for listed birth control and diabetes medicines, paid through deals with each province or territory. By mid-2026, four places had signed. Each deal runs for a set number of years.

items.title: MANITOBA
items.text: Signed first, in February 2025. Covers listed birth control and diabetes medicines, and menopause hormone therapy.

items.title: BRITISH COLUMBIA
items.text: PharmaCare Plan NP started on March 1, 2026, for listed diabetes medicines, birth control and menopause hormone therapy. More diabetes supplies were added on April 1.

items.title: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
items.text: Signed in March 2025. Check the province’s list for the exact birth control and diabetes products it covers.

items.title: YUKON
items.text: Signed in 2025. Covers listed birth control and diabetes medicines through Yukon’s own drug programs.

blocks.text: If you live anywhere else, national pharmacare does not pay for your prescriptions yet. Your provincial plan, a private plan or a program for high drug costs still decides what you pay. Where a deal exists, the product still has to be on the national list, so ask the pharmacist to check the exact brand and strength.

items.title: “National pharmacare means every prescription is now free.”
items.text: It is a first stage for two groups of medicines in the places that signed a deal. Your heart pill, inhaler or antibiotic still follows the usual plan rules.

sections.title: Dev and the Approval That Still Had a Deductible

blocks.text: Meet Dev
paragraphs: Dev Sharma lives in Surrey and has just been approved for a new medicine for his heart. His goal is to start it this week, as his doctor asked. The approval letter says his plan will now cover it.
At the pharmacy, Dev expects to pay nothing. The receipt, having received no such instructions, shows $310.
Dev is stunned. That is most of his grocery money for the month. He thinks about leaving the bag on the counter and trying again next month.

Instead, he asks the pharmacist one question: why? The pharmacist explains. The approval made the drug eligible, but Dev has not paid his Fair PharmaCare deductible yet this year. His income on file is also two years old, from when he earned more.

Dev decides not to skip the medicine. He pays for a one-week supply he can afford and asks his doctor about a lower-cost option the plan also covers. Then he updates his income with Fair PharmaCare that night.
The twist comes a week later. With his lower income on file, his deductible drops sharply. His next refill costs far less, and he knows exactly when the plan will pay more.
The medicine does not become magically free. The cost becomes something he can trace, and Dev has a plan for the deductible, the renewal and the next refill instead of a surprise at the counter.

items.title: AT THE COUNTER
items.text: $310, plan pays $0

items.title: THAT NIGHT
items.text: One-week supply, income updated

items.title: A WEEK LATER
items.text: Lower deductible on file

blocks.text: What resolved the conflict?
Approval and payment are separate steps. Check the deductible, your income details and the family maximum before you expect to pay nothing.
Dev kept taking his heart medicine by asking why it cost $310 instead of walking away from the counter.
blocks.detail: One question to your pharmacist can turn a shocking price into a plan you can afford.
blocks.extra: Section 06 gives you six safe questions for the counter.

sections.title: When You Cannot Pay for the Refill Today

blocks.text: A high price is a problem to solve with your pharmacist, not a reason to go without. A sudden jump can come from an expired approval, a reset deductible, old income details, a different product or two plans not talking to each other. Ask what changed, then work through these.
Six safe questions before you leave the counter

items.title: Price first
items.text: What will I pay today, and which part is the plan not paying?

items.title: Listed version
items.text: Is a generic, or a different strength, on my plan’s list when this one is not?

items.title: Short fill
items.text: Can you fill a few days now and the rest when I can pay?

items.title: Prescriber call
items.text: Can my prescriber switch me to a covered option, or ask for special approval?

items.title: Income review
items.text: My income dropped. How do I ask my plan to recalculate my deductible?

items.title: Support programs
items.text: Does the drug maker or a charity run a patient support program for this medicine?

blocks.text: Write down the answers and the date. If a plan turned down a claim, ask for the reason in writing and how to appeal. Pharmacists see these problems every day, and many fixes take one phone call from the counter.

items.title: “If I cannot afford it, skipping a few doses is the safe middle ground.”
items.text: Skipping or splitting some medicines can be dangerous. Talk to a pharmacist or prescriber first. They can often find a cheaper safe option faster than a missed dose can cause trouble.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is your health card not proof that pharmacy drugs are covered?
items.detail: Coverage for hospital and doctor visits is not the same as coverage for every drug at the pharmacy. Whether you qualify, signing up and the drug list still matter.

items.title: Which four kinds of payer should you check?
items.detail: A public plan, a federal program, a private plan and patient help programs.

items.title: What three parts can make up a pharmacy price?
items.detail: The drug cost, the pharmacy’s markup and a dispensing fee. Your plan pays its share of the parts it covers.

items.title: A family’s Fair PharmaCare deductible is $1,600, and it has paid $1,000 this year. How much more before PharmaCare pays 70%?
items.detail: $600. After that, PharmaCare pays 70% of eligible costs until the family maximum.

items.title: A household’s income after tax is about $50,000. Roughly what is its Trillium deductible?
items.detail: About $2,000 a year, which is about 4%, split into four quarterly amounts of roughly $500.

items.title: Does national pharmacare cover every prescription in Manitoba, B.C., PEI and Yukon?
items.detail: No. It covers listed birth control and diabetes products, plus menopause hormone therapy in some places. Other drugs follow the usual plan rules.

items.title: What does special approval do?
items.detail: It can make a limited drug eligible for the plan to pay. Deductibles, co-payments, price rules and other plans may still apply.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Prescription Coverage and Cost File

blocks.text: Use medicine and document names only. Do not write health card numbers, prescription numbers or health portal logins here.

Ask the pharmacist for the price before they fill it, and whether a lower-cost version is covered. Never skip, split, swap or stop a prescribed medicine only because of cost without first talking to a pharmacist or prescriber about safe options.
Covered is a list, not a price.
blocks.detail: Find who pays first, ask for the price before the fill, track your deductible and keep your income details current, so the plan you qualify for is the plan you actually get.

items.title: Formulary
items.text: The official list of drugs a plan covers, and its conditions.

items.title: Deductible
items.text: What you pay yourself before the plan starts sharing the cost.

items.title: Co-payment
items.text: Your flat fee or percentage for a covered claim.

items.title: Family maximum
items.text: The yearly amount after which the plan pays more of your costs.

items.title: Dispensing fee
items.text: The pharmacy’s charge for filling a prescription.

items.title: Special authorization
items.text: Medical approval needed before a limited drug is covered.

items.title: Generic substitution
items.text: Using a lower-cost version that works the same, under plan rules.

items.title: Coordination of benefits
items.text: How two or more plans share one claim, and in what order.

items.title: Plan NP
items.text: B.C.’s national pharmacare plan for listed diabetes, birth control and hormone therapy products.

items.title: Patient support program
items.text: Help from a drug maker or charity with the cost of a specific medicine.

quiz.question: True or False: “A provincial health card automatically pays for every outpatient prescription.”

questions: Which province or territory do you live in? Name your public drug plan if you know it.

Which medicine are you asking about? A name and strength are enough.
Did the pharmacy say it needs special approval or is not on the drug list? (Yes / No / Not sure)
About how much did you pay, or are you being asked to pay? An estimate is fine.
